parsed.hook: Brauneberger Juffer Sonnenuhr is not Mosel Riesling in the abstract; it is a steep slate wine from one of the valley’s most prized south-facing vineyard sites, and that matters because slate translates sunlight into ripeness while keeping the wine taut. In Auslese, Fritz Haag can take that site’s precision and turn it into a wine that reads as laser-cut fruit rather than weight.
parsed.wine_summary:
Fritz Haag sits in the small group of Mosel producers that treat sweetness as a tool, not a style crutch. That is the key to understanding this wine: Auslese here is about selecting very ripe berries from a site that naturally gives high acidity and low pH, so the wine can carry fruit concentration without turning cloying.

Brauneberger Juffer Sonnenuhr is a slope wine in the strictest sense. The combination of Devonian slate, steep exposure, and the Mosel’s cool river-influenced climate pushes Riesling toward lime peel, white peach, and a smoky mineral edge, while the best vintages bring enough density for the sweeter selection to feel layered rather than simple. This is the kind of bottle that rewards patience because the sweetness is only half the point; the other half is the cut of the acid and the salty slate finish.
parsed.terroir_expression: The Mosel’s cool continental climate, long ripening season, and steep slate slopes are the engine here: warm days help Riesling reach Auslese ripeness, while cold nights preserve acidity, so the wine tastes ripe but never heavy. Brauneberger Juffer Sonnenuhr’s slate and slope amplify drainage and heat retention, which is why the wine leans toward lime, green apple, and white peach wrapped around a smoky, flinty mineral line rather than toward tropical fruit.
parsed.vinification_summary: Auslese means selected ripe clusters, usually from fruit picked berry by berry or from especially ripe portions of the vineyard, and that concentration is what gives the wine its depth. At this sweetness level, residual sugar does not make the wine soft; it balances Mosel acidity, which is the internal wiring that keeps the wine lifted and prevents it from tasting thick.
parsed.food_pairing:
Hot Thai green curry with shrimp works because coconut milk and chile heat need sweetness, while Riesling’s acidity cuts the richness and keeps the curry from flattening the palate. 

Nashville hot chicken is a smart casual match: the wine cools the chile burn, and the fruit sweetness buffers the fried crust and spice oil. 

Peking duck with hoisin and scallions lands well because the wine’s acidity resets the palate after lacquered skin, while the sweet-sour sauce echoes the wine’s residual sugar. 

Foie gras torchon with apricot compote and toasted brioche is the fine-dining pairing that makes sense here; the wine’s acidity slices through fat, and the fruit bridges the sweetness of the compote. 

Aged Comté or cave-aged Gruyère with pear chutney works because the salt and nutty fat sharpen the Mosel slate note, and the chutney picks up the wine’s ripe stone-fruit register.
comparable_wines: Dr. Loosen Wehlener Sonnenuhr Riesling Auslese — similar Mosel slate, steep-site perfume, and balanced sweetness driven by acid.
JJ Prüm Graacher Himmelreich Riesling Auslese — comparable for cool-climate precision, smoky slate character, and long aging potential.
Egon Müller Scharzhofberger Riesling Auslese — richer in pedigree and price, but in the same lane of highly selective Mosel sweetness and cut.
parsed.style_profile: Sweet Mosel Riesling with high acidity, light body, and slate-driven smoky mineral lift
parsed.cellar_recommendation: Drink now if you want the vintage fruit and perfume, but this style gains complexity with bottle age as the sugar integrates and the slate note deepens. Store cool, dark, and steady; 8-12°C is ideal, and the best bottles can evolve for two decades or more.
parsed.value_assessment: $45-90 is the price range where this wine usually makes sense, and it is worth it when the bottle comes from a strong vintage and a reputable importer. At that level, compare it with JJ Prüm Auslese and Dr. Loosen’s top-site Auslese; Fritz Haag earns its keep through site precision, cleaner fruit definition, and a finish that feels more exact than plush.
parsed.market_position: This is a sommelier and specialist-retail wine first, not a casual supermarket buy. It lands on restaurant lists that care about German Riesling by vineyard, and it attracts collectors who know that Mosel Auslese is one of the clearest expressions of sweet wine with structure rather than sweetness alone.
parsed.insider_take: The tradeoff is simple: if you want hedonistic, broad sweetness, look elsewhere; this wine is about tension, not volume. What people miss is that Auslese from a site like Brauneberger Juffer Sonnenuhr is not dessert wine in the sugary sense — it is a structured wine that can make spicy food, blue cheese, and foie gras taste sharper and cleaner.
